title: Woe to the City of Blood
summary: Nahum pronounces woe on Nineveh as a city of blood, lies, and plunder, pictures its streets heaped with the slain, and compares it to a seductive harlot and sorceress who ensnared nations. God declares that he will expose and disgrace it, and asks whether Nineveh is better than Thebes, the great Egyptian city Assyria itself had destroyed. The chapter mocks the city's preparations for siege and ends by telling the king of Assyria that his wound is incurable and that all who hear of his fall will applaud.
story: Chapter 1 revealed God's character and decision; chapter 2 showed the attack. Chapter 3 gives the reasons and the final verdict. Nineveh falls because it is a city of blood, because it seduced and enslaved nations, and because its cruelty was constant. The chapter's comparison with Thebes is its argument in miniature: Assyria believed its strength made it safe, as Thebes had once believed, and Assyria had proved Thebes wrong. The book ends with a question addressed to the Assyrian king, and with no word of hope for Nineveh. That silence sends the reader back to Jonah, where God's last word to Nineveh was compassion, and makes the contrast between the two books the frame for understanding both.
historical:
Verses 8 to 10 refer to the sack of Thebes, which Nahum's Hebrew calls No-Amon, the city of the god Amun. Thebes, in upper Egypt on the Nile, was one of the grandest cities of the ancient world, the religious capital of Egypt for centuries. In the seventh century BC Egypt was ruled by a dynasty from Cush (Nubia, south of Egypt), which is why verse 9 names Cush and Egypt as Thebes's strength. The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal invaded Egypt and sacked Thebes around 663 BC, carrying off its treasures and people, an event recorded in Assyrian inscriptions. Put and Libya were peoples of North Africa allied with Egypt.

Nahum's audience would have known that Assyria had done to Thebes exactly what verse 10 describes: exile, the killing of children, captives divided by lot, and nobles in chains. Assyrian royal inscriptions and palace reliefs openly record such treatment of conquered cities. The final verse's reference to constant cruelty summarizes more than a century of Assyrian policy. When Nineveh fell in 612 BC, the other nations of the region had little reason to mourn it.
cultural:
The woe cry (hoy) that opens the chapter was the lament shouted at funerals, and prophets used it to announce judgment, as if mourning someone who was as good as dead. The picture of Nineveh as a harlot and mistress of sorcery (verse 4) combines two ideas. Prostitution here is a figure for the way Assyria lured smaller nations into alliances and vassal treaties that became traps, and sorcery points to deception and to the divination and magic for which Mesopotamia was known. Verse 5's threat to lift her skirts over her face draws on the ancient practice of publicly shaming a woman, and on the humiliation of captives, who were often led away stripped; the image is deliberately harsh and belongs to the prophetic vocabulary of disgrace (compare Isaiah 47:2-3 on Babylon).

The siege preparations in verse 14 reflect real practice. A city under siege needed stored water, and its walls, made largely of mud brick in Mesopotamia, needed constant repair, so defenders worked clay, trod mortar, and fired bricks in kilns. The locust images in verses 15 to 17 draw on a common experience in the Near East: swarms that appeared suddenly, stripped the land, and vanished when the sun warmed them. Nineveh's merchants, guards, and scribes, numerous as locusts, will likewise disappear.
literary: The chapter opens with a woe oracle (verses 1 to 7) whose first lines are among the most breathless in the Bible, a rush of nouns without verbs: whip, wheel, horse, chariot, horseman, sword, spear, slain, corpses. The effect is like a series of snapshots from the battlefield. God's direct speech (verses 5 to 7) repeats the formula Behold, I am against you from 2:13. Verses 8 to 13 form a taunt built on a rhetorical question and a historical comparison. Verses 14 to 17 are ironic commands, telling the city to prepare defenses that will fail, with a string of locust similes. Verses 18 and 19 address the king of Assyria directly and end the book, like Jonah, with a question. Jonah ends with God asking whether he should not care about Nineveh; Nahum ends by asking who has not felt Nineveh's cruelty.

outline.t: Woe to the city of blood, the seductive harlot
Fortresses like ripe figs, gates wide open
Prepare for siege: locusts that fly away
The king's shepherds asleep, the wound incurable

doctrines.note: Nineveh's judgment is tied to specific sins: bloodshed, lies, plunder, the seduction and enslavement of nations, and constant cruelty. God's justice answers the actual harm done, and the nations who suffered recognize it as just.

The comparison with Thebes teaches that no city's walls, water defenses, or allies can secure it against God's decree. Assyria had seen this truth when it destroyed Thebes, but failed to apply it to itself.

The chapter shows sin at the scale of an empire: violence organized as policy, deceit as diplomacy, and wealth built on the suffering of others. Sin is not only private; it can shape the life of a whole city.

words.note: Hoy, woe or alas. The cry came from funeral lament, and prophets used it to announce judgment on those whose conduct had doomed them. Habakkuk uses it five times in his taunt against Babylon (Habakkuk 2). Here it announces that Nineveh is as good as dead.

Zenunim, harlotry or prostitution. The prophets use this word most often for Israel's unfaithfulness to God, but here it describes Nineveh's seductive power over other nations, luring them with the promise of alliance and prosperity and then enslaving them. Revelation's picture of Babylon the great as a harlot draws on this prophetic tradition.

No, the Hebrew name for Thebes, from the Egyptian word for city; the fuller form No-Amon means city of Amun, its chief god. Jeremiah 46:25 and Ezekiel 30:14-16 also name it in oracles against Egypt. Nahum's appeal to it is an argument from history that his hearers could verify.

Ra'ah, to pasture or shepherd, here as a noun for the king's officials, your shepherds. Rulers were called shepherds throughout the ancient Near East. Assyria's shepherds sleep while the people scatter on the mountains with no one to gather them, the opposite of the ruler Micah promised who would stand and shepherd his flock (Micah 5:4).

christ: Nahum 3 does not predict the Messiah, but its imagery reaches the end of the Bible. Revelation 17 and 18 describe Babylon the great as a harlot who seduced the kings of the earth, grew rich through merchants, and deceived the nations by her sorcery, and whose fall is greeted by rejoicing in heaven. John draws on the prophetic oracles against Babylon, Tyre, and Nineveh to portray every empire that sets itself against God. The shepherdless people of verse 18 also form a contrast with Jesus, who saw the crowds harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd, and had compassion on them (Matthew 9:36). Where Assyria's shepherds slept and the people were scattered, Jesus presents himself as the good shepherd who gathers the scattered and lays down his life for the sheep (John 10). The link is thematic: Nahum shows what failed shepherds and violent power produce, and the gospel shows the kind of king God finally gives.

hard.q: Why does the book end with applause at Nineveh's destruction and no offer of mercy, when Jonah shows God sparing the same city?
hard.a: The difference between Jonah and Nahum is real and deliberate. Jonah shows that God's mercy extends even to Israel's worst enemy when that enemy repents. Nahum addresses a later situation in which Nineveh's violence has continued for generations, and it speaks to the victims rather than to the Assyrians. Some interpreters see the two books as a pair, showing the two sides of Exodus 34:6-7: God is compassionate and slow to anger, and he will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. Others emphasize that Nahum's applause comes from the nations who suffered, not from God taking pleasure in death, and they point to Ezekiel 18:23, where God asks whether he takes any pleasure in the death of the wicked. The book's closing question, who has not experienced your constant cruelty, invites the reader to weigh Assyria's conduct rather than simply to rejoice. Readers who find the ending hard are in good company; the canon itself keeps Jonah and Nahum together in the one Book of the Twelve.

questions: Assyria had destroyed Thebes but assumed it could never suffer the same fate. Where are people or nations tempted to think the lessons of history do not apply to them?
Nahum describes Nineveh's power as seductive, luring nations before enslaving them. What kinds of power work that way today?
Jonah and Nahum show God's mercy and justice toward the same city. How do you hold both of these together in your own picture of God?
